summary: Fewer young Chinese are chasing 'safe' government jobs, car sales are slumping at home, and tech giants race to sell AI helpers to offices and shoppers.
body: For years, a government job has been the dream of many young Chinese graduates because it is seen as stable. That may be shifting a little: about 3.45 million applicants were approved to sit the national civil service exam for 2027 jobs, down 7.2% from last year and the first drop in seven years, Caixin reports [^1]. Caixin links the fall to tighter screening of applicants. Competition is still fierce, with 35,700 openings, or about 97 applicants for each post [^1].

The wider economy is cooling. Factory activity shrank in October for the third time in four months, and economists blame weak spending at home after the early-October holiday [^2]. Car buying has slumped: retail sales of passenger cars fell 28% from a year earlier in September and 26% in the first 25 days of October, according to Caixin [^3]. Carmakers are leaning on exports; Geely says its overseas sales rose 169% in the first nine months of the year [^3]. Industries tied to AI and electronics are the exception and are booming [^2].

Shoppers are being courted with AI. Alibaba's Tmall expects a record one million brands in its Singles' Day sale, which peaks on November 11, and its Qwen-powered shopping assistant compares products and lets people try on clothes virtually [^4][^5]. At work, Tencent launched "Buddy One" on October 29, an AI workspace whose agent carries out office tasks across apps, competing with similar tools from ByteDance and Alibaba [^6].

Tech tensions with the US continue. On October 30 the US Federal Communications Commission voted to stop accepting safety tests from labs in countries without a testing agreement, including mainland China, starting in December 2028; Chinese labs handled most of these tests last year [^7]. China, for its part, now requires export licences for some AI technologies, though state media report that DeepSeek and MiniMax have been allowed to keep selling abroad [^8]. My read: the two countries are building separate tech systems step by step.
differences: Analysts quoted by Reuters expect China to meet its 4.5% to 5% growth target without new stimulus, while other economists call for more support for households, such as help with mortgage interest [^2]. The FCC rule is opposed by Beijing and by some US industry groups [^7].
